summary: On 29 May 2026, OpenAI reported degraded access across eleven currently listed ChatGPT components: Conversations, Login, Compliance API, Search, File uploads, Voice mode, GPTs, Image Generation, Deep Research, Agent and Connectors/Apps. OpenAI began investigating at 13:20 and declared all impacted services fully recovered at 13:28, an eight-minute public incident window. The provider did not disclose a technical root cause, affected-user count or regional distribution. The event began more than eight hours after an earlier login and account-creation incident had been resolved.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: The v0.8.0 review retains the record as unclassified. The broad ChatGPT component-access interruption is evidenced, but the reviewed sources do not establish a service-continuity requirement and its applicable functional threshold for these affected users at the event time. The OECD repair proposition concerns safe intervention mechanisms; it does not supply that missing availability threshold. No formal adoption prerequisite is imposed. The eight-minute notice window and eleven currently listed components do not establish actual onset, a common cause with the earlier same-day incident, or a customer-specific continuity threshold. Recovery alone establishes neither continuity compliance nor an access-state success.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: OpenAI's first-party incident page reports access issues across eleven currently listed ChatGPT components: Conversations, Login, Compliance API, Search, File uploads, Voice mode, GPTs, Image Generation, Deep Research, Agent and Connectors/Apps. The provider began investigating at 13:20 on 2026-05-29 and declared full recovery at 13:28. The public record establishes an eight-minute ChatGPT availability incident but does not identify the technical cause or quantify affected users. Its published window began more than eight hours after the earlier login and account-creation incident was resolved. The earlier account included ChatGPT Atlas in a twelve-component list. The current page lists eleven and omits Atlas; no historical capture establishes when that list changed.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The evidenced boundary is broad component availability, not a particular access-authority mechanism. A list of degraded components does not show that distinct access states were conflated, that an authentication transition failed to propagate, or that valid entitlement depended on an unavailable verifier. The provider's investigating and resolved updates preserve the operational sequence, while the absent cause prevents a more specific taxonomy adjudication. Event separation is also substantive: two status incidents on the same date should not be merged when their published windows do not overlap and no common cause is disclosed. The material episodes retain resolved-no-mapping dispositions. Breadth and temporal proximity do not establish a specific governance mechanism or common cause, and no success mapping is inferred from recovery alone. The fully adjudicated unclassified result preserves that distinction. No eligible FC-derived or independently source-identified admitted requirement is established by this bounded status report; absence of a finding does not establish compliance. Independent occurrence-level external assessment finds affirmative, source-bounded repair in the reported restoration stage. Relevant communication/incident-process requirements remain Boundary where the decisive plan or implementation record is not public. Requirements addressing a different technical object, lifecycle or source date remain audit-only; voluntary adoption is not a gate. The current-edition availability review separately tests the existence and scope of a continuity requirement. The sources do not establish the affected users’ applicable functional threshold or required recovery response. The independent repair assessment is preserved; its safe-intervention proposition does not itself establish a service-availability threshold. This is an evidence-bounded no-mapping result, not a conclusion that the provider had no obligations.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: This incident demonstrates that component breadth and mechanism specificity are different questions. CAM can require clear status scope and event separation while withholding an access-governance classification until causal evidence identifies the actual failed boundary. This avoids turning same-day proximity or a long affected-component list into unsupported mechanism attribution.
